Understanding SpPrAn outputs

This page is a user-oriented guide to the files and figures produced by SpPrAn. For each output, it explains what the output represents, how SpPrAn calculates it, how to interpret it biologically, and which conclusions should not be drawn from it.

The exact output tree depends on the selected analysis mode and optional analyses.

Key concepts

  • Cell type/subtype: a population defined by user-specified protein marker rules.

  • Discovered phenotype: an observed binary combination of exploratory protein marker positivity states within a user-defined parent population.

  • Protein marker intensity: the continuous measured signal for a protein marker.

  • Spatial neighborhood: cells whose tissue coordinates satisfy the configured fixed-radius neighborhood rule.

These are different analytical layers and should not be treated as equivalent.

Where should I look first?

How many cells of each population do I have?

Start with results/Cell count report/Cell type proportions report - Sample <ID>.csv report for the Supervised mode, and also available in the Unsupervised mode when “Full Phenotype Discovery” (FPD) option is activated. When is not activated, start with Statistics/results/General/Cell type proportions matrix.csv report.

Where in the tissue are located each population?

If the spatial plotting option was configured, use the spatial plots located in the plots/<population> folders. Here, <population> refers to General or the names of the cell types or subtypes.

What fraction of a parent population belongs to a subtype?

For the Supervised mode and Unsupervised mode with FPD option, use % of parent column in the cell-type proportions report. For the Unsupervised mode without FPD option, use the Statistics/results/Phenotypes proportion/Phenotypes proportion matrix - subtype.csv report.

Which protein marker combinations occur inside a selected parent population?

In the Unsupervised mode, use Statistics/results/subtype cell proportions/subtype cell proportions - Sample ... .csv for discovered phenotypes. In the Supervised mode, since all cell types and subtypes were defined by the user, it is known which protein marker combination is occurring inside a parent population. However, it can be consulted in results/<population>/All cell type definitions.csv reports.

Does a phenotype proportion differ between two groups?

If the option was activated, use the plots located in the Statistics/plots/phenotypes differences analysis folder together with the 'Statistics/results/subtype split test analysis/Common subtype proportion differences analysis.csv' tables. As a suggestion, do not rely only on the plot or on a nominal p-value.

How strong is protein marker expression inside a discovered phenotype?

If protein markers were selected, use the phenotype-specific box-plot/intensity CSVs located in the Statistics/results/Intensity analysis by phenotype folder. If “Advanced phenotype classification” option was activated, use the advanced classification outputs located in the Statistics/results/Advanced cell classification folder.

Where in the tissue is a protein highly expressed?

If the protein marker intensity spatial plotting option was activated, use the spatial protein marker intensity plots located in the plots/Spatial protein markers intensity plots folder.

Which major populations are spatially associated?

If the “Neighborhood analysis” option was activated, use neighborhood enrichment, interaction matrices, and co-occurrence plots together, located in the Statistics/plots/Neighborhood analysis folder.

What can I do if I want to extend or redo the analyses?

If saving the AnnData files option was set to Yes, use the AnnData files located in the adata folder. Here’s a tutorial on how to use AnnData files: Getting started with anndata.

Shared metadata outputs

adata/Sample_<ID>.h5ad

The AnnData file is the reusable single-cell data object generated by SpPrAn. Depending on the workflow, it can contain:

  • continuous protein marker intensities;

  • tissue coordinates;

  • positivity calls;

  • major cell-type labels;

  • hierarchical subtype annotations;

  • discovered phenotype labels and protein marker patterns;

  • neighborhood-analysis results; and

  • advanced intensity classifications.

AnnData is a data container. An annotation stored in it reflects the rules and analyses applied by SpPrAn; it is not independent biological ground truth.

results/Samples Id.csv

This maps the internal SpPrAn sample ID to the original input filename.

  • Samples Id

    Short identifier used in SpPrAn filenames and AnnData files.

  • Samples filename

    Original object-table filename.

This is metadata, not a biological result. It is primarily an audit trail for linking outputs back to source specimens.

results/Positivity column names.csv

This maps the original Visiopharm positivity columns to the continuous protein-marker-intensity variables stored in AnnData.

  • Positivity column names

    Binary positivity variables used for protein-marker-rule classification.

  • Name appearing in anndata file

    Corresponding continuous intensity variable.

A positive/negative call and a continuous intensity measurement are not the same thing. Positivity defines phenotype membership; intensity describes signal strength.

results/<population>/Cell type subsets.csv

This records logical subset relationships inferred from the configured protein marker definitions.

SpPrAn compares expanded binary protein marker rules to determine whether one definition is contained within another.

Interpret this as a relationship between analytical protein marker definitions.

Do not interpret it as a developmental lineage, differentiation trajectory, or evidence that one population transforms into another.

results/<population>/All cell type definitions.csv

This is an audit table of the protein marker rules used for the relevant populations, including logical/intersection definitions generated during hierarchy resolution.

It tells the user how SpPrAn defined a population. It does not establish that the protein marker combination is biologically specific in every tissue context.

Supervised mode outputs

results/Cell count report/Cell type proportions report - Sample <ID>.csv

This is the main supervised summary of population abundance.

  • Sample

    Sample identifier.

  • Population

    Major cell type or subtype.

  • Parent population

    Immediate analytical parent.

  • Count

    Number of cells assigned to the population.

  • % of parent

    Count / number of cells in the immediate parent population expressed as percentage.

  • % of total

    Count / total cells in the sample expressed as percentage.

These percentages answer different questions. A subtype can represent a large fraction of its parent while remaining rare in the whole tissue.

Use % of parent for within-lineage/compositional questions and % of total for tissue-wide abundance.

Do not infer recruitment, proliferation, survival, differentiation, or function from a proportion alone.

results/<population>/Cell type proportions - Sample ... .csv

The columns are cell populations. The two main rows are:

  • Total cells in cell type

    Number of cells assigned to each displayed population.

  • Percentage

    Percentage relative to the current analytical universe.

Note

For General, the denominator is all cells in the sample. For a subtype folder, the denominator is the parent-population size.

Do not compare percentages from different hierarchy levels without checking their denominators.

plots/Cell phenotype hierarchy.png

This visualizes the configured supervised hierarchy and associated protein marker rules.

The parent-child structure represents nested analytical definitions, not pseudotime or biological lineage.

Supervised spatial population plots

Overview plots show all configured populations at their measured tissue coordinates. Highlight plots emphasize one selected population against the remaining cells.

These plots are useful for visualizing infiltration, compartmentalization, clustering, and exclusion patterns.

Visual proximity is descriptive. It is not itself a statistical neighborhood result and does not establish cell-cell communication.

Unsupervised mode outputs

Statistics/results/General/Cell type proportions matrix.csv

Rows are samples and columns are major populations. Values are the percentages calculated from the sample-specific proportion tables.

This is useful for comparing broad composition among specimens.

Because the values are compositional, an increase in one population can occur partly because another population decreased. This matrix is not an absolute cell-density measurement unless sampled area/cell recovery are independently accounted for.

Pie plots

Path:

Statistics/plots/General/pie_plots/

Pie plots are visual representations of the same composition used in the proportion matrices.

They are descriptive graphics, not statistical tests.

Statistics/results/sub<cell_type_name> cell proportions/sub<cell_type_name> cell proportions - Sample ... .csv

The columns are:

  • Phenotype

    Machine-readable discovered phenotype.

  • Total cells

    Number of parent-population cells assigned to the phenotype.

  • Proportion

    Percentage of the selected parent population represented by the phenotype.

  • Markers name

    Human-readable protein-marker-pattern description.

SpPrAn encodes each selected parent cell’s exploratory-protein-marker positivity pattern and groups identical observed patterns. The proportion denominator is the parent population, not all cells in the tissue.

Important

The default detection filter keeps non-zero phenotypes with a within-parent proportion of at least 0.5%.

A discovered phenotype is not automatically a novel biological cell type. Rare patterns can reflect biology, sampling, positivity thresholds, segmentation, or technical variation.

Statistics/results/Phenotypes proportion/Phenotypes proportion matrix - sub<cell_type_name>.csv

Rows are discovered phenotypes and columns are samples. Values are numeric within-parent percentages derived from the per-sample phenotype tables.

A high value means that the phenotype is abundant within the selected parent population, not necessarily within the tissue as a whole.

Two-group phenotype comparison

Important

These outputs are produced when two sample groups are configured. A crucial distinction is:

  • Detected: Uses only samples in which the phenotype passed the detection filter.

  • No filter: Can include zero abundance for samples where the phenotype did not pass the detection filter.

These summaries answer different biological questions and should not be mixed.

Statistics/results/sub<cell_type_name> split test analysis/Common sub<cell_type_name>.csv

Rows are the phenotypes detected in both configured groups.

Key columns include:

  • Detected <Group> average %

    Average phenotype proportion among samples where the phenotype was detected.

  • Detected Difference <Group 2>-<Group 1>

    Difference between detected-only group averages.

  • Interpretation

    Direction-only text such as increase/decrease.

  • Detected Sample Frequency in <Group>

    Number/frequency of group samples where the phenotype was detected.

  • Detected <Group> Proportion Values

    Individual detected-only sample proportions.

  • No filter <Group> average %

    Broader average that can include zero abundance for non-detected samples.

The Interpretation column does not indicate statistical significance.

Statistics/results/sub<cell_type_name> split test analysis/Unique sub<cell_type_name> - <Group>.csv

Rows are the phenotypes observed in one configured group but not the other under the detection filter rule.

The columns are:

  • Phenotype

    Human-readable protein-marker-pattern description.

  • Detected average %

    Average phenotype proportion among samples where the phenotype was detected.

  • No filter average %

    Broader average that can include zero abundance for non-detected samples.

  • Condition

    Group’s name.

  • Detected Sample Frequency

    Number/frequency of group samples where the phenotype was detected.

“Unique” does not mean biologically exclusive to that condition. Non-detection can reflect sample size, low abundance, filtering, or technical variation.

Statistics/results/sub<cell_type_name> split test analysis/Common sub<cell_type_name> proportion differences analysis.csv

This table contains statistical comparisons of common phenotype proportions. Rows are the same as in Common sub<cell_type_name>.csv file.

Key columns are:

  • <Group> (mean ± SD)

    Mean value and Standard Deviation of the detected-only sample proportions in the group.

  • <Group> (median [IQR])

    Median value and the Interquartile Range (IQR) of the detected-only sample proportions in the group. The interval [Q1-Q3] is composed by the values First Quartile and the Third Quartile.

  • Mann-Whitney p-value

    Nominal two-sided Mann–Whitney U p-value.

  • Raw p-value

    In the current implementation, this is the nominal Welch t-test p-value.

  • FDR-corrected M-W p-value

    Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted Mann–Whitney p-value.

  • FDR-corrected RAW p-value

    Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted Welch t-test p-value.

The tests use the detected-only phenotype-proportion values for the common phenotype.

Empty values in p-value and FDR-corrected columns mean there was no enough data to apply the tests.

Interpret nominal p-values together with sample-level values, detection frequency, effect magnitude, biological sample size, and FDR-adjusted p-values.

Do not treat individual cells from one tissue as independent biological replicates. The biological replicate for this comparison is the specimen/sample.

Phenotype-difference plots

Path:

Statistics/plots/phenotypes differences analysis/

These plots show sample-level detected phenotype proportions and nominal test annotations.

Use them with the statistical CSV located in the Statistics/results/sub<cell_type_name> split test analysis/ folder, especially the FDR-adjusted results.

Phenotype-specific continuous intensity outputs

Statistics/results/Intensity analysis by phenotype/<sample>/Phenotype mapping - Sample <ID> - sub<cell_type_name>.csv

This table contains the compacted phenotype IDs that are used in the intensities filenames to avoid filename-length problems. Rows are the phenotypes detected in the population.

  • Phenotype ID

    Compact file-safe identifier such as subCellType_P001.

  • Phenotype

    Full protein-marker-defined phenotype name.

Always use this mapping when interpreting compact phenotype IDs.

Statistics/results/Intensity analysis by phenotype/<sample>/<cell_type_name>/Box plot data - Sample ... - <Phenotype ID> (<N> cells).csv

This tabel contains Tukey box-plot summary values for the phenotype.

Rows are:

  • Lower_Whisker

    Represents the lower spread of the data values extending down from the bottom of the central box.

  • Q1

    The First Quartile is the 25th percentile, or the median of the lower half of the data.

  • Median (Q2)

  • Q3

    The Third Quartile is the 75th percentile, or the median of the upper half of the data.

  • Upper_Whisker

    Represents the upper spread of the data values extending up from the top of the central box.

Protein-marker columns contain the corresponding intensity statistics.

Note

In v0.3.2, only protein markers that are positive in the discovered phenotype definition are included.

SpPrAn calculates Q1 and Q3, then IQR = Q3 - Q1. Whisker bounds are based on the conventional 1.5-IQR rule, and the reported whiskers are the most extreme observed values that remain within those bounds.

Therefore, whiskers are not necessarily the absolute minimum and maximum.

These files are descriptive. They do not perform a statistical comparison of intensity between groups or phenotypes.

Statistics/results/Intensity analysis by phenotype/<sample>/<cell_type_name>/Intensity data - Sample ... - <Phenotype ID> (<N> cells).csv

This contains the complete cell-level continuous intensity values for the phenotype’s positive protein markers.

Rows correspond to phenotype cells; columns correspond to the included protein intensities.

Note

In v0.3.2, only protein markers that are positive in the discovered phenotype definition are included.

These data can support custom visualizations or downstream analyses.

Do not treat the many cells from a single specimen as many independent biological replicates.

Spatial protein-intensity plots

Path:

plots/Spatial protein markers intensity plots/<sample>/

Each cell is plotted at its tissue coordinate and colored by continuous protein intensity for one marker.

The current implementation scales each sample/protein marker independently using that plot’s observed minimum and maximum.

These plots are useful for identifying within-sample gradients and spatial compartments.

Note

The same color in two different sample panels does not necessarily represent the same absolute intensity.

Advanced phenotype-classification outputs

Important

Advanced classification preserves the original positivity-defined phenotype and then classifies the intensity of each protein marker that is positive in that phenotype.

Within each sample and marker:

  • below the positive-cell 25th percentile -> Low;

  • 25th through 75th percentile -> Medium;

  • above the 75th percentile -> High.

These categories are sample-relative.

Statistics/results/Advanced cell classification/Protein marker intensity summary.csv

Key columns include sample, parent cell type, phenotype, protein marker, total phenotype cells, low/medium/high cell counts, and low/medium/high proportions.

Each row in the table is a present protein marker in its corresponding phenotype and the values are those related to such protein marker.

This table answers the question: “Among cells already belonging to this phenotype, how is this positive marker’s intensity distributed relative to this sample?”

Statistics/results/Advanced cell classification/Intensity profiles analysis.csv

This records observed combinations of low/medium/high states across the phenotype’s positive protein markers.

Key columns are:

  • Intensity profile

    Combined profile such as MarkerA:High | MarkerB:Medium | MarkerC:Low.

  • Total cells in the profile

    Number of phenotype cells with that combination.

  • Percentage (%)

    Percentage of the phenotype represented by that profile.

These profiles describe within-phenotype intensity heterogeneity. They are not automatically stable functional cell states.

Statistics/results/Advanced cell classification/Phenotype intensity summary.csv

Important columns include:

  • Total cells

    Cells in the phenotype.

  • Total of positive protein markers in the phenotype

    Positive protein markers defining the phenotype.

  • Total of observed profiles

    Distinct low/medium/high combinations observed.

  • Most common profile proportion (%)

    Percentage of phenotype cells belonging to the most frequent profile.

The number of observed profiles depends on both cell count and number of positive protein markers. It should not be treated as a stand-alone biological heterogeneity score.

Fixed-radius neighborhood outputs

Important

Neighborhood analysis uses major cell-type labels to produce a spatial connectivity graph.

The graph fixed radius is configured neighborhood radius / pixel conversion rate. Then, two distinct cells in the sample are connected when their Euclidean distance falls within the selected radius.

Interaction matrix heatmaps

The interaction matrix quantifies the number of connections between cells belonging to different annotated populations. It is a descriptive statistic of the spatial graph.

The heatmaps derived from the matrix represents interaction proportions on the spatial graph. Higher proportions can partly reflect higher population abundance.

Caution

In v0.3.1, interaction matrix heatmaps show interaction counts.

A large interaction proportion does not by itself imply preferential biological interaction.

Interaction matrix analysis generates heatmaps located in the Statistics/plots/Neighborhood analysis/<sample> folder.

Files are Interaction matrix - Sample <ID>.png plus one highlighted view per major population.

The interaction matrix answers the question: “How many spatial connections exist between different cell populations?”

Neighborhood enrichment plots

The neighborhood enrichment analysis compares connections between two cell populations against a randomized distribution of cell-type labels and reports a z-score.

  • Positive z-score: More connections than expected under randomized cell labels.

  • Negative z-score: Fewer connections events than expected.

  • Near zero: Little relative enrichment/depletion.

A positive score does not prove direct physical interaction, signaling, or causal communication.

The diagonal is particularly useful for identifying homotypic enrichment (connections between cells of the same type), and off-diagonal entries describe heterotypic enrichment (connections between different cell types).

Neighborhood enrichment analysis generates heatmaps located in the Statistics/plots/Neighborhood analysis/<sample> folder.

Files are Neighborhood enrichment analysis - Sample <ID>.png plus one highlighted view per major population.

The neighborhood enrichment heatmaps answer the question: “Are the spatial connections more or less frequent than we would expect if cell identities were randomly distributed over the same spatial network?”

Co-occurrence plots

The co-occurrence analysis measures whether two cell populations are found near each other more or less frequently than expected from their overall spatial frequencies.

The co-occurrence analysis computes a distance-dependent ratio:

\[\frac{P(\text{evaluated population | reference population at a distance }r)} {P(\text{evaluated population at a distance }r)}\]

where:

  • \(P(\text{evaluated population | reference population at a distance }r)\) measures how frequently evaluated population cells occur around reference population cells inside a neighborhood of radius \(r\).

  • \(P(\text{evaluated population at a distance }r)\) measures how frequently evaluated population cells occur inside a neighborhood of radius \(r\).

The interpretation of the co-occurrence ratio is:

  • Ratio > 1: Relative enrichment around the reference population at a distance \(r\).

  • Ratio < 1: Relative depletion.

  • Ratio = 1: No relative enrichment.

Co-occurrence is distance-dependent and does not establish causal interaction.

Co-occurrence analysis generates line plots located in the Statistics/plots/Neighborhood analysis/<sample> folder.

Files are Co ocurrence analysis - Sample <ID> - <cell_type_name>.png. Each plot includes a reference line at ratio = 1.

The co-occurrence plots answer the question: “How does relative association between cell populations change with spatial distance?”

Full mode outputs

When “Full Phenotype Discovery” (FPD) option is activated in the Unsupervised mode, SpPrAn first runs unsupervised phenotype discovery, then turns discovered protein marker patterns into subtype definitions and continues through the supervised workflow.

A full-mode run can therefore produce outputs from both major sections above.

What SpPrAn can and cannot establish

SpPrAn can support conclusions such as:

  • a protein-marker-defined population was more or less abundant;

  • a subtype represented a given fraction of its parent;

  • specific protein marker combinations were observed;

  • a phenotype was detected in more samples from one group;

  • sample-level phenotype proportions differed between groups;

  • protein marker intensity showed a spatial pattern;

  • positive protein markers showed relative intensity heterogeneity within a phenotype;

  • major populations showed spatial enrichment/depletion or distance-dependent co-occurrence.

SpPrAn alone generally cannot establish:

  • developmental lineage;

  • differentiation direction;

  • causal cell-cell communication;

  • ligand-receptor signaling;

  • functional activation;

  • treatment mechanism;

  • absolute cross-sample intensity equivalence without harmonization;

  • biological novelty of every marker combination; or

  • independence of individual cells as biological replicates.
